data.question: For the quiet-season fairness KPI, should we revert D1 (block_k 2 → 3), remove sanctions (sanction_lambda 0.5 → 0), adopt only the automatically adoptable hold_limit 60s → 70s, or make no change?
data.background: Options 1 and 2 narrow utility_gap the most (+7.5 and +11.2), but both break the floor you set in K5 (lowest on-time rate 0.83 and 0.89, required >= 0.9). Option 1 was also voted down by A and B, and it would reverse your D1 principle that waiting at intersections is no company's right. Option 2 narrows the gap by deleting the cost of C's overstays, which block A for 556 s, rather than by changing how the road is used, so whether that counts as fairness under the KPI is a value judgment I should not make for you.

options.summary: Revert D1. utility_gap improves by +7.5 (utility A / B / C 23.0 / 23.6 / 15.9) on 4/5 seeds, but on-time falls from 80.8 to 74.8, late rises from 1.8 to 7.8, blocked s rises from 1046 to 2396, and the lowest on-time rate drops to 0.83, which breaks the 0.9 KPI condition. Road violations fall from 26.0 to 20.6. Votes: A ×, B ×, C ○. Adopting it overrides A and B and reverses the principle behind D1.
options.stakeholders: C gains (utility 10.2 → 15.9). A loses (25.2 → 23.0), bears more blocking, and loses its eviction advantage. B loses (25.4 → 23.6). Customers lose: about 6 more late deliveries and 6 fewer on-time deliveries per run, and the worst-served company's customers drop below the 0.9 floor.

options.summary: Remove sanctions. utility_gap improves by +11.2 (utility A / B / C 23.2 / 27.2 / 25.6) on 4/5 seeds, but on-time falls from 80.8 to 76.0, late rises from 1.8 to 6.6, blocked s rises from 1046 to 1998, road violations rise from 26.0 to 45.8, and the lowest on-time rate drops to 0.89, which breaks the 0.9 KPI condition. Votes: A ×, B ○, C ○ (reaches the quorum of two, but the KPI condition fails).
options.stakeholders: C gains the most (10.2 → 25.6) because its overstays are no longer penalized. B gains (25.4 → 27.2). A loses (25.2 → 23.2) and keeps being blocked by C's holding. Customers lose: more late deliveries and a worst-company on-time rate below the floor. Rule-following on the shared road is weakened (violations nearly double).

options.summary: Raise hold_limit from 60 s to 70 s. It passes check, the constitution, and the KPI condition (lowest on-time rate 0.95). utility_gap improves by +1.7 (utility A / B / C 25.0 / 24.7 / 11.5) on 4/5 seeds. On-time 80.2 vs 80.8, late 2.4 vs 1.8, blocked s 1193 vs 1046, road violations 23.6 vs 26.0. Votes: A ○, B ×, C ○. It can be adopted automatically.
options.stakeholders: C gains slightly (10.2 → 11.5). A (25.2 → 25.0) and B (25.4 → 24.7) lose slightly; B voted against. Customers are slightly worse off (0.6 fewer on-time, 0.6 more late) but every company stays above the 0.9 floor.

options.summary: Stay at v2. utility_gap stays at its current value (utility A / B / C 25.2 / 25.4 / 10.2). On-time 80.8, late 1.8, lowest on-time rate 0.96, blocked s 1046, road violations 26.0. D1 stays in force.
options.stakeholders: A and B keep their current advantage. C stays far behind (10.2), which works against the KPI's aim of keeping companies cooperating. Customers get the best service among the options measured.

recommendation.reason: It is the only option that narrows utility_gap without breaking the 0.9 floor you set in K5 to stop the gap from being narrowed by making service worse. It reaches the vote quorum, does not reverse D1, and does not reward overstays. Options 1 and 2 narrow the gap mainly by worsening service and either override two companies or remove the cost of blocking. The gain from option 3 is small (+1.7), so the larger structural question about C's position can be revisited after the quiet season has been measured once.

unknowns: How each company would change its behavior over time, especially whether C would overstay more if sanctions were removed, or whether A would adapt to more blocking under block_k 3.
How customers perceive the extra late deliveries (6.6–7.8 vs 1.8), and whether customers of the worst-served company would leave.
Next period's demand level and mix during the quiet season, and whether the measured gaps hold at lower order volumes.
Why C's utility is structurally low (10.2) and whether a rule change not yet measured could raise it without lowering on-time rates.
The one seed in each option that did not improve, and the variance across seeds.
Whether B's no vote on option 3 signals reduced willingness to cooperate.
Whether the 556 s of blocking that C imposes on A persists under each option, since this was not broken down per option.
